description: Somos Los Perdidos, un equip que se perdió en los datos de la NASA y encontró el camino.
summary:
Pachama-map for Cochabamba is a farmer-first decision-support web app that helps smallholders in the peri-urban valley of Cochabamba, Bolivia, choose crop rotations that conserve water and protect soil health. Farmers register their parcel on a satellite map, the crops they grow, their water availability and their priorities: saving water, improving soil, income or forage.

The tool combines NASA POWER observations with SoilGrids soil properties, FAO-56 crop coefficients and a catalog of six traditional valley crops. From these it compares the farmer's current rotation with four alternatives. NASA POWER contributes both the long-term monthly climatology (rainfall, frost days, solar radiation) and recent root-zone soil moisture with its anomaly. For each strategy the tool estimates the irrigation it would need, its frost exposure and the months the field would sit bare. It scores water, soil, climate risk, income and forage, and explains in plain Spanish why the strategy was suggested, what evidence supports it, its benefits, what is still unknown, and which risks need local review.

Rainfall in the valley is concentrated in three months, frosts are frequent and planting decisions are made by habit. Pachama-map turns NASA data into clear, explainable choices that support, never replace, farmer judgment.
details:
What it does

Pachama-map is a web-based decision-support system built around the farmer's parcel, for three pilot zones in Cochabamba: La Maica, Albarrancho and northern Tunari.

  1. Farmer registration and parcels. A four-step sign-up designed for farmers: personal details and community; drawing the parcel boundary on a satellite map; crops currently grown; and water source, water availability, soil type (optional) and priorities. Farmers can manage several parcels, each with several crops.
    • NASA POWER daily data gives temperature, precipitation, humidity and model-based surface and root-zone soil moisture (GWETTOP/GWETROOT, MERRA-2). The tool compares current soil moisture with the long-term normal for that month and reports the anomaly.
    • The NASA POWER monthly climatology gives rainfall, minimum and maximum temperature, frost days and solar radiation. It is shown as a 12-month calendar that highlights wet, dry and frost-prone months: the seasons when crops are most vulnerable.
    • SoilGrids (ISRIC) adds soil texture, plant-available water capacity and drainage. Farmers can override these with their own knowledge.
    • schedules each crop in its local sowing window and detects bare-field months;
    • estimates crop water use as reference evapotranspiration × the FAO-56 crop coefficient for each growth stage. Reference evapotranspiration comes from NASA POWER solar radiation (Hargreaves–Samani). Irrigation need is that crop water use minus effective rainfall and the soil's available water;
    • measures frost and heat exposure against each crop's tolerance, drainage mismatches and water demand beyond the farmer's availability;
    • scores five criteria (water, soil health, climate risk, income, forage), weighted by the farmer's priorities. Soil health rewards nitrogen fixers, ground cover, organic matter, deep roots and a change of plant family between cycles to break pest cycles, and penalizes bare months.
  2. Short-term outlook. A 14-day forecast feeds a 7- and 14-day water balance that uses each crop's FAO-56 crop coefficient. Days with heavy rain (≥ 30 mm) are flagged for drainage review.
  3. Per-crop fit recommendation. Each crop gets an explainable 0–100 fit score based on the forecast and rotation compatibility.
  4. Historical explorer (public landing page): NASA GIBS MODIS imagery for any date since 2000, and NASA POWER daily series for any period, both for La Maica.
  5. IoT digital twin. Farmers choose the devices they own (irrigation valve, greenhouse vent, fan, mister, shade net, sensor). A live control room shows an animated greenhouse, gauges, manual controls, and automation rules derived from crop thresholds. It has manual, automatic and pause modes, red highlighting of out-of-range readings, pop-up alerts, and demo scenarios (heat wave, drought, frost). All devices are emulated.

Benefits and intended impact.

  • Farmers can see, before planting, how much irrigation a rotation would need and when their fields would sit bare or exposed to frost.
  • They can see which options rebuild soil through legumes and ground cover, and which fit their own goals.
  • Water and soil decisions move from habit to transparent evidence.
  • Municipal technicians can use the same explanations in conversations with farmers.

Tools and technologies.

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, Leaflet / React-Leaflet (Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap basemaps), lucide-react.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, pytest.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose with Nginx.
  • Data: NASA POWER (daily and climatology APIs), NASA GIBS (MODIS), SoilGrids 2.0 (ISRIC), FAO-56 crop coefficients and rooting depths, Open-Meteo forecast, and a curated catalog of six Andean valley crops: alfalfa, sweet corn, potato, onion, fava bean and forage oat.
  • Hardware: none required (IoT is emulated).

Creativity. The tool links three things usually built separately: Earth-observation climate data, agronomic rotation logic and an IoT digital twin. A farmer can go from "what should I plant next?" to "how would I protect it automatically?" in one place. Every score is broken down and justified, so the farmer sees why a strategy is suggested, not only which one.

Factors we considered.

  • Farmer-first, Spanish-language design for users with limited technical experience; responsive layout for mobile phones.
  • Honesty about data limits. NASA POWER describes a ~0.5° regional cell, not a field. Soil moisture comes from a model. When the live soil query is slow, a real reference soil profile is used. Crop attributes and sowing calendars are orientative and flagged for validation by local experts.
  • Graceful degradation: real archived NASA samples are used when APIs fail, and the user is told.
  • Clear reminders that the tool supports, but does not replace, farmer judgment and local agronomic expertise.
